draft.title: Interpreting abstract ideas
card: An abstract idea, such as freedom, loss or justice, cannot be seen or touched. A text often shows it through images, events and characters instead of stating it plainly.
Questioning
asking what the text means by an idea and why the author chose a particular image or event.
Connecting
linking the idea to other parts of the text, to other texts, or to your own knowledge of the world.
Inferring
working out meaning that is not stated, by combining clues in the text with what you already know.
draft.remember: Combine questioning, connecting and inferring, and check your reading against the words on the page.

a.q: A poem never uses the word grief. It describes a woman setting the table for two each night, then sitting alone. What is the reader doing when they decide the poem is about grief?
opts: Inferring meaning from clues the poem gives
Questioning the poet's choice of title
Connecting the poem to a different text
Copying a definition of grief into notes
a.why: The poem does not state grief, so the reader works it out from the clues of the table and the empty seat. That is inferring. Connecting would need a link to another text or experience, which the question does not mention.
a.clue: The idea is never stated, so it must be worked out.

b.q: Leila reads a story in which a lighthouse keeper keeps the lamp lit though no ships pass. She asks why the author chose a lamp, then recalls a novel where a lit window means hope. She decides the lamp stands for hope. Which strategies has she combined?
opts: Questioning, connecting and inferring
Questioning and summarising only
Connecting and predicting only
Inferring and paraphrasing only
b.why: Leila questions the choice of a lamp, connects it to the lit window in another novel, and infers that it stands for hope. The other options leave out at least one of these steps. Nothing in her reading is summarising, predicting or paraphrasing.
b.clue: Count each step Leila takes, from asking to deciding.

a.best: Inferring meaning from clues the poem gives

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the only one without 'only', the only one naming three strategies, and the only one using exactly the three strategies the card teaches. Every distractor includes a strategy the card never mentions (predicting, paraphrasing, summarising), so a student can pick it by recognition without analysing Leila's steps.
The remember line adds 'check your reading against the words on the page', which the card never teaches. It also tells students to 'combine' the strategies, while the card only lists them separately.

b.q: Leila reads a story in which a lighthouse keeper keeps the lamp lit though no ships pass. She asks why the author chose a lamp, then recalls a novel where a lit window means hope. She decides the lamp stands for hope. Which part of her reading is connecting?
opts: Recalling a lit window in another novel
Asking why the author chose a lamp
Deciding that the lamp stands for hope
Reading that no ships pass the lighthouse
b.why: Recalling the lit window links the story to another text, which is connecting. Deciding the lamp stands for hope is tempting, but that step works out an unstated meaning, so it is inferring. Asking why the author chose a lamp is questioning.
b.clue: Which step links the story to something outside it?
